surveyDefinition.title: Skin Care Products — consumer survey (Germany)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, ingredient and efficacy priorities, and switching behaviour.

segments.name: Concern-Treatment Consumers
segments.description: Buy skincare to treat a specific, often persistent skin concern (acne, hyperpigmentation, sensitivity, menopause-related changes). They research ingredients and are willing to try clinical or derm-recommended products, but are frustrated by irritation and lack of visible results.

segments.name: Prevention-Focused Buyers
segments.description: Use skincare primarily to prevent aging and maintain skin health. They are quality-led, value efficacy backed by evidence, and are open to premium or clinical products if they deliver visible anti-aging benefits.

segments.name: Minimalist Maintenance Users
segments.description: Keep a simple, low-effort routine focused on basic cleansing, moisturising and sun protection. They are not deeply engaged in the category, are price-conscious, and avoid complex multi-step regimens.

segments.name: Clean-Conscious Shoppers
segments.description: Seek products with natural, clean, or sustainable credentials, but also demand efficacy. They are sceptical of greenwashing and need trustworthy certifications, and are willing to pay a premium for clean formulations that work for their sensitive skin.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skin Care Products buyers in Germany. It asks how people use Skin Care Products, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Germany who buy or use Skin Care Products for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. Excluded: Professional buyers (e.g., dermatology clinics, spas, salons) purchasing for resale or professional use; Individuals purchasing solely as gifts for others; Children under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly purchases skin care products (e.g., cleansers, moisturizers, serums, sunscreens)
Researches products online, reads reviews, follows influencers or dermatologist recommendations
May have specific skin concerns (acne, aging, sensitivity, hyperpigmentation)
Brand loyal but open to switching for better efficacy or price
Purchases through multiple channels: drugstores, department stores, specialty beauty retailers, e-commerce, subscription boxes
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's skincare world: which products they use, their skin concerns, and how complex their routine is. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger to decision, including where they learn and buy, and what ultimately drives their choice. Next, it probes their expectations and trade-offs, especially around efficacy, clean ingredients, and price. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and future intentions, revealing where they are likely to switch or invest next.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Skin Care Products in Germany — who Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. This captures the core B2C market and allows for segmentation by demographics, skin concerns, and purchasing behavior.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, ingredient and efficacy priorities, and switching behaviour.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of Jobs-to-be-Done and Usage/Behavioural: the category is split by the primary job the routine is hired to do (prevent aging, treat a concern, maintain basic health, or simplify) and by how deeply engaged the routine is — this separates buyers more meaningfully than price sensitivity or

segments.name: Concern-Treatment Consumers
segments.description: Buy skincare to treat a specific, often persistent skin concern (acne, hyperpigmentation, sensitivity, menopause-related changes). They research ingredients and are willing to try clinical or derm-recommended products, but are frustrated by irritation and lack of visible results.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report higher routine complexity, higher spend on targeted serums/treatments, and will switch brands frequently in search of efficacy.

segments.name: Prevention-Focused Buyers
segments.description: Use skincare primarily to prevent aging and maintain skin health. They are quality-led, value efficacy backed by evidence, and are open to premium or clinical products if they deliver visible anti-aging benefits.
segments.hypothesis: This group will prioritise anti-aging claims and be willing to pay more for proven ingredients like retinol or peptides, and will show high loyalty to products that deliver results.

segments.name: Minimalist Maintenance Users
segments.description: Keep a simple, low-effort routine focused on basic cleansing, moisturising and sun protection. They are not deeply engaged in the category, are price-conscious, and avoid complex multi-step regimens.
segments.hypothesis: This group will report low routine complexity, low spend, and will be driven by convenience and value for money rather than efficacy claims.

segments.name: Clean-Conscious Shoppers
segments.description: Seek products with natural, clean, or sustainable credentials, but also demand efficacy. They are sceptical of greenwashing and need trustworthy certifications, and are willing to pay a premium for clean formulations that work for their sensitive skin.
segments.hypothesis: This group will prioritise clean beauty claims and sustainability, but will switch away from brands that fail to deliver efficacy or that engage in greenwashing.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question bb6 (Which of these matters most when you choose a skincare product?) is the tie-breaker because it directly asks respondents to rank their top priority, and the top-ranked option (clinically proven results vs. targeted for a specific concern vs. natural ingredients vs. price) cleanly separates the four segments based on their core motivation.
notes: Minimalist maintenance users are identified by low product count, low engagement, price sensitivity, and lack of specific concerns.
Concern-treatment users are identified by specific concerns (acne, hyperpigmentation), use of treatments/serums, and prioritization of targeted solutions and dermatologist input.
Prevention-focused users are identified by anti-aging concerns, use of eye cream/serum, and prioritization of clinical evidence and visible results.
Clean-conscious users are identified by sensitivity concerns, preference for natural/clean ingredients, and prioritization of certifications and sustainable packaging.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's skincare world: which products they use, their skin concerns, and how complex their routine is. It then follows their purchase journey from trigger to decision, including where they learn and buy, and what ultimately drives their choice. Next, it probes their expectations and trade-offs, especially around efficacy, clean ingredients, and price. It closes with satisfaction, unmet needs, and future intentions, revealing where they are likely to switch or invest next.
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'usage frequency' with 'routine complexity' as a key engagement metric, because in skincare the number of steps and products used is more differentiating than simple frequency of application.
Added 'skin concerns and goals' as an early beat to capture the jobs-to-be-done lens, which is essential for separating segments like Concern-Treatment vs Prevention-Focused.
In the buying section, placed 'spend' last as a sensitive item, and included 'discovery' early because European consumers heavily research online before buying.
In preferences, added 'claims and certifications' to address the region's growing clean beauty and sustainability concerns, and 'trade-offs' to reveal how they balance efficacy vs clean vs price.
In satisfaction, added 'unmet needs and frustrations' to capture pain points like greenwashing and irritation, which are key to switching behaviour.
All beats are designed to be answered with closed questions and avoid asking age, income, or geography directly.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
